title: Google Review Card Design And Copy Guide
summary: A design and copy playbook for Google review cards that balances tap instructions, QR fallback, brand identity and the realistic dwell time customers spend looking at the card — so the lead action is always obvious even when branding is strong.
heroPoints: A review card has to explain the action inside three seconds — before it has earned the right to look premium or on-brand.
Design should support tap, scan and brand recall in that order; competing cues reduce action rates, not increase them.
The strongest first design almost always comes from one clear lead action with a secondary fallback — not three equal choices.
imageAlt: Google review card design mockup with tap instruction and QR fallback

sections.title: Why design is a conversion decision, not a brand decision
sections.intro: Most review-card revision cycles stall because the design team treats the card as a micro brand asset, while the operations team treats it as a tool for getting reviews. Both framings are right, but they point to different layouts.
bullets: A review card lives in a moment of compressed attention: three to eight seconds between a customer finishing service and choosing what to do next. Branding only works if the action is understood first.

The card is held in one hand and read at arm's length, often in mixed lighting (warm lobby lamps, cool countertops, outdoor patios). Type that looks crisp in a mockup can become illegible in that real environment.
Conversion-first design does not mean ugly design. The best cards read as premium because the action is obvious — clarity feels confident, ambiguity feels amateur.

sections.title: The layout hierarchy that actually works
sections.intro: A review card has roughly three bands of attention. Getting the hierarchy right is the difference between a tap rate that feels natural and one that needs a staff prompt every time.
bullets: Top band — promise and action: a short line that tells the customer what happens when they tap. 'Leave us a Google review — tap or scan' is clearer than 'We'd love to hear from you.' The action verb is non-negotiable.

Middle band — visual affordance: an NFC tap icon with a phone silhouette, plus a QR code sized at a minimum of 2 cm square. Both affordances together teach the customer how to use the card without reading instructions.

Bottom band — brand and reassurance: logo, business name, and one reason to bother ('help a local café stay open', 'a 30-second review helps us a lot'). Brand lives here because it only matters once the customer has decided to engage.
Avoid edge case: QR codes below 2 cm are unreliable from most phone cameras at natural card-reading distance. Test at 40 cm, not 10 cm.
Avoid edge case: NFC tap icons placed near the corner often invite taps on the wrong face of the card. Centre the tap target visually, and ideally place the antenna where the icon suggests.

sections.title: Copy that survives real customer attention
sections.intro: The copy on a review card has to be readable by a tired guest, an elderly customer, and a tourist whose first language is not your brand's language. That constraint rules out most of the clever phrasing a creative team wants to try.
bullets: Keep the main line under eight words. 'Scan or tap to leave a Google review' works; 'Your voice helps our little family-owned shop thrive in difficult times' does not.
Use an imperative verb. Tap. Scan. Leave. Share. Not 'consider leaving' or 'we appreciate if you could'.
Name the platform. 'Google review' converts better than 'review' because customers recognise the brand and trust the destination.
Keep the secondary line practical, not emotional. 'Takes about 30 seconds' beats 'means the world to us'.
Avoid jargon. 'Tap here' is clearer than 'Engage NFC prompt'. 'Scan the code' beats 'Scan the QR'.
Internationalise carefully. In markets with mixed language customers, a short bilingual line is better than a dominant-language line with a smaller translation.

sections.title: Visual system: icons, type and colour contrast
sections.intro: The visual system is where most review cards fall apart in real placements. A design that looks crisp in RGB can lose its affordance once it is printed on a reflective laminate under a warm incandescent bulb.
bullets: NFC icon: use the Wi-Fi-style arc plus a phone silhouette. A generic contactless symbol alone is too abstract for many customers.
QR code: minimum 2 cm square, quiet zone of at least 4 mm, high contrast between code and background. Reverse-contrast codes (light on dark) work but need 20% larger sizing to scan reliably.
Type: sans-serif, minimum 10 pt for the main line, minimum 7 pt for secondary. Serifs and decorative faces read as 'fancy branding' and dilute the action.

Colour contrast: target WCAG AA (4.5:1) between headline copy and card background. Many premium brand palettes (cream on gold, silver on white) fail this test; fix the card even if the broader brand keeps the palette.
Finish interaction: gloss lamination creates glare under lobby spotlights. Matte or soft-touch laminate reads more reliably in mixed lighting.
Dark mode bias: phones are often viewed in auto-dark mode. Cards with light text on dark backgrounds still read fine; cards with low-contrast mid-tones become unreadable.

sections.title: Balancing brand identity against the action
sections.intro: The hardest conversation in review-card design is about how much brand can live on the card without hiding the action. These are the principles that tend to survive that conversation.
bullets: Brand lock-up stays on one face — usually the front. The back face carries the tap or scan affordance with less brand overlay.
Pattern elements (background textures, gradient washes) belong on the edges, not behind the action. A decorative element that forces the action copy down to 8 pt is the wrong trade.
Colour: the brand's accent colour is a great home for the NFC icon and the QR frame. Using it to highlight the action aligns brand and conversion instead of fighting them.
Photography: if the card carries a photograph, reserve it for the back face. Photographs on the action face almost always reduce tap rate.
Debadging: resist the urge to remove the 'Google' wordmark for design cleanliness. Customers recognise Google trust more than they recognise your logo; hiding it costs more than it gains.

sections.title: Proof review and sample validation
sections.intro: The proof round is where design decisions meet printed reality. Running it well turns design into decision faster than any mockup can.
bullets: Print two to four variants: the current favourite, one more conversion-first variant, one more brand-first variant. Compare in the real placement, not on a design review call.
Test QR scan at 40 cm on three phones: a modern iPhone, a modern Android, and a three-year-old mid-range Android. If any of them misses, sizing or contrast needs to change.
Test NFC tap with the card face down on a bag, face up on a counter, and held at waist height. Antenna location matters — some cards only tap reliably when held in a specific orientation.

Read-aloud test: hand the card to three people who have never seen it and ask them to describe what they would do next. If they do not say 'tap' or 'scan' inside two seconds, redesign the action line.
Lighting test: review the card under warm white (3000K), cool white (4000K) and daylight (6500K). Colour contrast that passes under one lighting condition can fail under another.

sections.title: Multi-location and franchise consistency
sections.intro: A single-store review card decision is a design problem. A multi-location card programme is a system problem, and system problems need more rules than a single card does.
bullets: Template kit: a locked hierarchy with editable location name, review URL and optional accent colour. Franchisees customise inside the template; they do not redesign the template.
QR URL per location: each card points to the specific Google Business Profile for its location. Central URL-shortening or tracking wrappers are fine; generic brand URLs are not.
Language packs: for international brands, publish the template in the three to five most common customer languages. Local teams pick the language pack, not the layout.
Central approval: the template requires central brand approval before print. Local customisations (address line, phone number) do not.
Measurement baseline: every location reports review volume lift from the first 90 days of the card programme. Laggard locations get coaching on placement and staff prompt, not a new card design.

faq.question: What should be most visible on a review card design?
faq.answer: The action line. 'Scan or tap to leave a Google review' — with a visible NFC icon and a QR code of at least 2 cm square — is the most visible element on every high-performing card. Brand lives below the action, not above it. Customers only engage with branding after they understand what the card does.

faq.question: Should review cards include both NFC and QR?
faq.answer: Yes, in almost every case. NFC is faster for customers who know how to tap; QR is a reliable fallback for customers who do not, phones with NFC disabled, and staff demos at a distance. The design still needs one lead affordance so the customer is not confused — usually NFC as primary with QR as a smaller secondary mark.

faq.question: How small can the QR code be?
faq.answer: 2 cm square is the reliable minimum for phones held at natural card-reading distance (about 40 cm). Go smaller only if the card is always held in hand and the design maintains a 4 mm quiet zone plus high contrast. Anything under 1.5 cm fails often enough to hurt the conversion numbers.

faq.question: What type size is safe for the main action line?
faq.answer: 10 pt sans-serif at minimum for headline copy, 7 pt for secondary. Serif and decorative faces read as branding rather than instruction and reduce tap rate. Test readability at 40 cm under warm lobby lighting — the distance and lighting where the card is actually read.

faq.question: How much brand colour can live on the action face?
faq.answer: Enough to signal identity without reducing contrast on the action copy. Target WCAG AA (4.5:1) between headline and background. Many premium palettes (cream-on-gold, silver-on-white, light tints on light tints) fail contrast; fix the card even if the broader brand keeps the palette.

faq.question: Should the card say 'Google review' or just 'review'?
faq.answer: Always 'Google review'. Customers recognise the Google brand and trust the destination more than they trust an unnamed review platform. The word 'Google' consistently raises conversion in comparison tests, and hiding it for design cleanliness costs more than it gains.

faq.question: What is the single biggest avoidable mistake in review-card design?
faq.answer: Letting brand identity dominate the action. The card has three to eight seconds of customer attention; if the brand is the first thing the eye lands on, the action is already lost. Design the action first, drop the brand in around it, and only increase brand presence if the action still reads as obvious.
